newsitem.title: USA: Ex-SAS security group joins up with Florida firm.
newsitem.headline: Ex-SAS security group joins up with Florida firm.

text.p: Armor Holdings Inc. can count on the skills and expertise of former members of Britain's elite SAS regiment with its acquisition of British security consultant Defence Systems Limited (DSL).
Senior DSL executives are veterans of conflicts from the Falkland Islands to the Middle East, staff members said Tuesday.
The company operates in such potentially rich but definitely dangerous places as Colombia and Algeria.
Armor Holdings, based in Jacksonville, Fla., makes and supplies security equipment such as flak jackets, bulletproof vests and anti-riot gear for police and military forces.
The main business of DSL, whose London headquarters are close to Buckingham Palace, is advising multinational companies and other clients on security in high-risk areas and in training personnel.
Armor Holdings announced its aquisition of DSL for $26 million earlier this month.
DSL Cairman Alistair Morrison and Chief Executive Richard Bethell are both former member of the famed SAS.
"They have very distinguished service records," a DSL executive in London, who asked not to be identified, said in a telephone interview Tuesday.
In keeping with the air of mystique the SAS cultivates, he declined to confirm all the details of their military records.
But Morrison won the Military Cross, one of Britain's highest awards for valour, in 1973, for his service with the SAS in Oman.

He received the Order of the British Empire (OBE) for his role in the rescue of hostages from a Lufthansa airliner hijacked to Mogadishu, Somalia, by Palestinian guerrillas in 1977, press reports say.

Bethell was an officer in the Scots Guards, a top infantry regiment, and served with the SAS in the 1982 Falklands War against Argentina. News reports say he was involved in the TWA hijacking in Beirut. He was decorated as a Member of the British Empire (MBE).
DSL was set up in 1981. Since then, the security consulting field has boomed as companies find working in countries designated "emerging markets" is often fraught with risk.
DSL works particularly with mining and petrochemical companies in the Third World.
"We don't generally operate in developed countries. There's little call for our expertise," the executive said.
DSL advises on security in Colombia, where left-wing guerrillas have attacked oil installations operated by British Petroluem and kidnapping for profit is rife.
It also works in Algeria, where Islamic rebels are fighting army-backed authorities in a conflict the executive described as "particularly horrible ... quite unlike anything else."

In Angola, it has organised protection of diamond fields which were a valued prize in the long war between the government and Jonas Savimbi's UNITA (National Union for the Total Independence of Angola) rebels.
DSL has also recruited former members of the Gurkhas, the legendary fighting men from Nepal who serve in the British Army, to act as guards at British embassies.
The executive stressed that, unlike some international security firms, it was not involved in the mercenary business.
"We facilitate security by providing management. We are not talking about groups of armed men," he said.
